name: Emeka Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers or government. Your answers stay confidential. How does an ordinary working day go?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43, studied music at university and have accompanied singers for years. I teach six piano pupils, record simple practice tracks and play for the choir; the fee is still low for what the week asks.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What keeps you in it, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like when a singer trusts my next chord without looking over. My partner works hospital porter shifts that move week to week, and two school-age children and a mortgage mean I count every paid date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the choir AI Plateau might make my booking list neater, but our Tuesday rehearsal still needs someone to follow each singer. I would keep the piano lesson slots and paid accompaniment dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI every day to sort rehearsal notes and draft scales, then play each one myself. Our mortgage is large against my low pay, my partner’s hospital porter shifts vary, and we have less than one month saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d confirm six beginner piano lessons and the two choir fees this week. If the choir pays both dates, I’d put ten into a new emergency envelope after the mortgage clears rather than buying another microphone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious already, though the tool itself does not frighten me here. A cancelled choir date means choosing which household bill waits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is one choir date worth?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One choir date buys about a week of groceries for our two children. The church’s thanks cannot be taken to the food shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the AI tool decide for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use the tool to put dates in order, not to decide whether a child can play a scale. The piano tells me when the printed exercise is wrong.

say: I’d tell the choir **live rehearsal** and piano lessons still need a player who listens.
I would accept a tidier **booking list** while asking for paid deposits.
think: Our **mortgage** and variable porter shifts leave less than a month of expenses saved.
I check every AI **scale draft** at the piano before a pupil uses it.
do: Confirm six **piano pupils** and two choir fees this week.
Save **ten** into a new emergency envelope only after both choir dates pay and the mortgage clears.
feel: I feel **anxious** because one cancelled choir fee would leave a household bill waiting.
fieldNote: His **baseline mortgage worry** follows from low pay, variable partner shifts and a nearly empty reserve.
He uses AI **daily** but tests exercises at the piano before handing them to children.
S0.quote: The church’s thanks cannot be taken to the food shop.

steps.text: Confirm six piano pupils and two paid choir dates this week
Save ten after both choir dates pay and mortgage clears

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell choir parents Steady Disruption could take cheap rehearsal tracks and client messages before live singers lose their accompanist. I would ask the studio which paid tracks it still wants from me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rehearsal-track recordings bring about a third of my music pay, and a generated piano part is cheap. We cannot cover the mortgage from my partner’s uncertain porter shifts if those fees vanish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the studio this month for written paid track dates. If one of my two monthly blocks disappears in the first year, I’d have the choir director show me a new AI score-alignment feature on music I own, then offer one paid evening rehearsal clinic only if the hall has a room and five families pay enough for hire and my time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m alarmed because a third of my pay is not loose change in this house. I can test a clinic, but I cannot put a made-up booking on the mortgage form.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is score alignment new for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI for notes already, but I have never used score alignment to match a singer’s live timing to a recording. The director would need to approve the sample and stand beside me for the first check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes the clinic pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five paid places cover the hall room and my evening at the current rate. I would not schedule a clinic for four families, even if they all say they love the idea.

say: I’d ask the **studio** for written paid tracks as cheap rehearsal recordings spread.
I would keep **live choir work** separate from generated practice audio.
think: Rehearsal tracks bring about **one-third** of my pay and may vanish.
Uncertain porter **shifts** cannot carry the mortgage alone.
do: Ask the **studio** this month for written paid recording dates.
Learn **score alignment** after one lost block only on owned music with director approval and a supervised first check.
Offer one paid **rehearsal clinic** in year one only with a room and five families covering hire and time.
feel: I feel **alarmed** because a third of my pay could vanish before we build savings.
fieldNote: His daily AI use covers **notes**, while score alignment is genuinely new supervised learning.
The **clinic** requires a room, five paid places and enough fees to cover his own time.
S1.quote: I cannot put a made-up booking on the mortgage form.

steps.text: Ask studio for written paid rehearsal-track dates this month
Learn score alignment after lost block on owned music with director supervising first check
Offer clinic after lost block if five paid places cover hall hire and my teaching time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the choir AGI by 2028 could write practice parts, answer clients and make rehearsal tracks as well as I do. Capable robots for hands-on playing would arrive around 2031, so live piano work has a later deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the studio to stop buying my simple tracks in 2028, and the choir could buy a generated rehearsal part too. Less than a month of bills saved means the mortgage could be late before I replace those hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the studio now for paid dates and the choir for a signed term schedule. If track orders end in the first year after 2028, I’d give notice on the rented recording room at its renewal, keep my six pupils, and ask the lender about temporary terms before arrears only if our cash falls short; I’d read the total interest cost with my partner before signing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because the studio part of my income could go quickly. The 2028 invoice may already be empty while my hands still know the piano.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where could you rehearse after leaving the room?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The room lease has a notice period, and I would follow it rather than pay a penalty. I can use the choir’s piano for paid rehearsals only if the director grants that time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not promise my children a cheaper mortgage. I would tell them their lessons are booked for this term and wait for the lender’s written answer before changing our plans.

say: I’d warn that **2028 thinking AGI** reaches tracks before capable playing robots around 2031.
I would ask for a signed **choir schedule** while live work still pays.
think: I expect simple **track orders** to stop, and even choir rehearsal work may shrink.
Less than one month of **savings** makes a fast fee loss dangerous for the mortgage.
do: Get paid **studio dates** and a signed choir term schedule now.
Leave the rented **recording room** at renewal if orders end after 2028; keep six pupils.
Seek **lender terms** if cash falls short after 2028; review full written interest cost with partner before agreeing.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about likely recording loss and an empty 2028 invoice.
fieldNote: He knows **thinking AI** can take tracks in 2028 while capable piano robots follow around 2031.
Room notice and **lender relief** depend on lost orders, lease terms and a real cash shortfall.
S2.quote: The 2028 invoice may already be empty while my hands still know the piano.

steps.text: Get paid studio dates and signed choir term schedule now
Leave recording room at renewal if track orders end after 2028
Review full written interest with partner before lender relief if cash falls short after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the choir AGI by 2031 gives us five years to see which families still want a pianist in the room. Capable robots for hands-on playing would follow around 2034, so I would use that gap to strengthen live teaching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could become a better group accompanist, but I cannot assume the choir pays for one. Our mortgage and thin savings mean any course needs a clear paid use and cannot replace the lessons I teach now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask two nearby choirs this winter for written paid accompanist requirements and ask the college whether a short group-leading course is funded. I’d enrol only if a choir accepts it, the grant covers fees, my partner can collect the children and classes miss no paid lessons; in the first year after 2031, I’d apply only if qualified and a posted net rate covers travel, mortgage and childcare, keeping pupils until an offer arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious about recording fees, but five years lets me check the course rather than buy hope. The bills still arrive every month while I learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the choir need from the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the choirs whether they require the course for a paid role, not merely like seeing certificates. I will not pay tuition for a badge with no opening behind it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would classes fit your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner’s hospital shifts change weekly, so I would confirm pickup for every class night before enrolling. If the rota cannot cover it, I would wait for the next intake rather than miss paid lessons.

say: I’d ask choirs for **paid role requirements** before taking a funded course.
I’d tell families **2031 AGI** reaches tracks before capable robots arrive around 2034.
think: A **group-leading skill** helps only if a choir funds paid work for it.
Tuition, childcare or lost **lessons** could worsen our mortgage pressure.
do: Ask two **choirs** for posted role requirements and the college about a grant this winter.
Enrol only in an **accepted course** with full funding, confirmed pickup and no lost paid lessons; otherwise wait next intake.
Apply in first year after **2031** only if qualified and posted net pay covers travel, mortgage and childcare; keep pupils until offered.
feel: I feel **anxious** about recording income with time to check an affordable route.
fieldNote: His **adaptive** response is a funded, accepted course tied to actual paid choir requirements.
Changing hospital **shifts** make childcare and preserved lesson pay necessary before training.
S3.quote: I will not pay tuition for a badge with no opening behind it.

steps.text: Ask choirs for paid requirements and college for group-leading grant
Enrol only if accepted course grant covers fees pickup confirmed and paid lessons remain
Apply first year after 2031 if qualified and posted net pay covers travel mortgage and childcare
Keep current pupils until a paid choir offer arrives

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell our children AGI by 2036 gives us ten years to plan our work, with capable robots for hands-on playing around 2039. I would still get the next choir fee signed this week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I might lead a paid choir or still teach piano, but neither fee is in our account today. Our mortgage and less than a month saved make the present week more important than a long forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep six pupils and signed choir dates this year, then put fifteen from each paid studio block into a new reserve only after the mortgage and food clear. Over the coming years I’d test a group rehearsal only if five paid families cover the room and my time. In the first year after 2036, I’d keep that group only while those fees still cover costs, and apply for a posted paid choir lead role only if I meet its requirements and net pay covers travel and childcare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about this month’s bills, even with a decade to change course. Ten years will not keep the lights on if the next choir date is cancelled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the fifteen be new savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fifteen would be new savings, not the mortgage money in another envelope. If the studio does not pay a block, I would save nothing from it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the children to finish their studies and make music because they love it. I would also show them a real invoice before calling a hobby a job.

say: I’d tell the children a **decade** gives room to plan before 2036 thinking AGI.
I would still get **choir fees** signed before debating robots around 2039.
think: At 53 a paid **choir role** is possible but not income today.
Our **mortgage and thin savings** keep this week’s fees important.
do: Keep six **pupils** and signed choir dates; save fifteen only from paid studio blocks after essentials.
Test a **group** only with five paid families covering room and time; keep it after 2036 while those fees hold.
Apply for a posted **choir lead** role after 2036 only if qualified net pay covers travel and childcare.
feel: I feel **anxious** about current bills despite a long warning.
fieldNote: His **new reserve** adds actual paid block fees after essentials, not a relabeling of mortgage cash.
A future **choir lead** role needs a posted paid opening, qualifications and net pay after travel and childcare.
S4.quote: Ten years will not keep the lights on if the next choir date is cancelled.

steps.text: Keep six piano pupils and signed choir dates this year
Save fifteen from paid studio blocks after mortgage and food clear
Test group with five paid families covering room and time; keep after 2036 while fees hold
Apply first year after 2036 for posted choir lead if qualified net pay covers travel childcare

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because practice-track orders could stop before the choir pays more live hours. Written dates, a room I can leave without penalty and clear lender terms if cash falls short would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask whether I enjoy all the new tools. I enjoy a tool that saves me an hour. My children still need the paid hour more than I need a clever screen.

headlineQuote: My children still need the paid hour more than I need a clever screen.
portrait: At **43**, Emeka is an experienced piano accompanist, teacher and recording musician with a bachelor’s degree in music.
Low **music pay**, variable hospital shifts and less than a month saved strain a mortgage household with two children.
He uses AI **daily** for notes, then tests new score alignment only with owned music and supervision.
Fast **2028 AGI** threatens practice tracks before capable piano robots arrive around 2031.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end practice-track orders before live choir pay replaces them.
whatWouldHelp: Written **dates**, penalty-free room notice and clear lender costs if cash runs short would help.
